newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Germans rally to save the Little Traffic-Light Man.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Germans rally to save the Little Traffic-Light Man.

text.p: In Europe's push towards broader unity, many steps along the way have sent citizens to the barricades. But no one is fighting the onslaught with more panache than supporters of east Germany's traffic light men.

The European Union, in an effort to standardise traffic lights, has insisted that Germany install gender-neutral, abstract stick figures in place of the cheerful little men, introduced in the 1960s under East German communist rule.
The proposed extinction of these beloved figures has rallied both east and west Germans in a country where traffic signals are shown particular deference.
German pedestrians wouldn't dream of crossing the street against a red light, even when there isn't a car in sight, for fear of setting a bad example to children.
While Germans revere traffic lights in general, they have a special attachment to the jolly signals of the former east.

Modelled after a stout turn-of-the-century German townsman, the beloved "Ampelmaennchen," as he is called here, cuts a striking figure at intersections with his broad-brimmed hat, spread-armed "stop" pose and chirpy "go" stride.

The endangered illuminated figures have achieved a kind of cult status throughout the country with their image emblazoned across T-shirts, hats, watches, posters and lamps. They even have their own pop song.
The threat to the diminutive figure has brought east and west Germans together to resist the EU's encroachment -- and their campaign seems to be working.
THE LITTLE MAN AND HIS FANS

"We never expected that the reaction would be so overwhelming," said Joerg Davids, founder of the Save the Little Traffic Light Man Committee, which has focused Germans' grumblings into a lobby group with its own Internet web site.

The EU version, which Juergen Heyer, Saxony-Anhalt's traffic minister, called "a sexless creature with a golf-ball head," has replaced 1,600 of the original 2,600 traffic signals in other eastern states.
Committee members say the rest will disappear within three years if more states do not act now to secure them.
Thanks to the efforts of the committee and local politicians, the remaining little green and red men are now protected in the states of Saxony and Saxony-Anhalt.

Part of the attraction of the little figure, with his spirited Prussian goosestep "go" movement and commanding "stop" stance, may be its role as an informal mascot of the East German state, which disappeared with unification in 1990.

Germans call such nostalgia for life in former East Germany "Ostalgie" -- a pun on the German word for east, "ost", and nostalgia -- but the affection for the little man has spread across to the other side of the fallen Berlin Wall too.

"I'm from the West and I have a case of Ostalgie," read one entry on the committee's web site which has been visited 150,000 times since its debut in September and has received messages from as far afield as the United States and Britain.

"The Little Traffic Light Man lives! Down with imperialist western traffic lights!!" "My little son is thrilled every time he sees the Little Traffic Man and I want to hold onto that feeling for him," two Germans said in messages to the site.

"Not everything in East Germany was or is bad!" "Traffic lights from East Germany are more dynamic and lively than the western ones. Why has everything got to be new?" said other messages to the web site.
But other people object to the campaign. "How can a symbol of East Germany be deified in this way? It makes me sick," read one message.
TRAFFIC SIGNALS AND POLITICS

Although the committee insists it is pursuing no overtly political message by protecting a symbol of East Germany, eastern officials have been quick to recognise the political advantage to be gained from rescuing the treasured signals.
The state of Saxony's economics minister, Kajo Schommer, became a local hero by ensuring the continued presence of the little men in his home state.
"We shouldn't imitate all the nonsense that comes from Bonn or Brussels," Schommer said.
The campaigners also argue that the east German traffic light man is more eye-catching and therefore safer.
The designer of the original Ampelmaennchen, cartoonist Heinz Behling, insisted that his lively little man increased street safety for children and the elderly.
But proponents of the EU switch say the traffic lights have to be replaced anyway because the old ones are corroded and incompatible with computerised traffic controls.
More than 80 million marks ($50 milllion) have already been spent on conversion to the new EU signals.
Committee members suggest that inexpensive stencils in the form of the Ampelmaennchen could be inserted in the new units for little additional cost.

Committee founder Davids hopes to organise an exhibition at the committee's headquarters with every European country's own unique traffic light men as a signal that local diversity is alive and well in the EU.
